verdict.reasoning: REFUTED — leading-whitespace / page-break furniture with zero content difference. Both halves of the claim's description are factually accurate; they simply do not add up to a content discrepancy. WHAT I SAW IN THE RENDER (E:/Temp/specrecon/v961/spec_p961.png, 2550x3300 @300dpi, read directly): the printed page does carry three indentation levels. '5.' and '6.' begin roughly 0.23 in to the RIGHT of 'c)' (~70 px at 300 dpi, about 2-3 character cells), so 5/6 sit at the deep sub-item level continuing 1.-4. from page 960, while 'c) Otherwise,' sits at the shallower a)/b) level under rule 1). WHAT I SAW IN THE MARKDOWN (specs/ISO_COBOL.md:38456-38472, measured with a whitespace dump): every content line of page 961 is at indent=0, whereas page 960 (lines 38410-38453) puts 'a)'/'b)' at 3 spaces and '1.'-'4.' at 6. The indent reset is real. It nevertheless fails every test for a reportable discrepancy: (1) NOTHING IS MISSING OR ALTERED. I compared the page word for word. Items 5 and 6 in full, 'c) Otherwise,', '(FUNCTION LENGTH (argument-1) + 1).', the 'NOTE These errors include, but are not limited to:' lead-in, and all three dashed bullets ('argument-1 is zero-length,' / 'argument-1 contains only spaces,' / "argument-1 contains valid characters but is incomplete, such as the string ' +.'.") are present, verbatim, in the same order. No rule, operand, qualifier, or choice indicator is lost. The claim alleges no textual difference at all — its own pdf_says and markdown_says quote identical prose. (2) NO MEANING CHANGES, because the hierarchy is carried redundantly by the enumerators, and those transcribe correctly. '5.' and '6.' follow '4.' in unbroken numeric sequence, so they can only continue that nested list; 'c)' follows 'a)' and 'b)' in unbroken alphabetic sequence, so it can only be their sibling under rule 1), and its 'Otherwise,' has no other possible antecedent. The claim's stated harm — 'c) look[s] like a top-level item' — is unreachable: 15.95 contains no top-level 'c)' anywhere, and 15.95.4 has exactly one numbered rule, '1)'. Note too that 'a)'/'b)' on page 960 are not CommonMark list markers either (alphabetic markers are not list syntax); they are paragraph text. So 'c)' at column 0 is not being demoted from a real list level to a fake one — it was never a list item. (3) IT IS SYSTEMIC PIPELINE BEHAVIOR, NOT A PAGE-961 DEFECT. I scanned all 1261 page anchors in specs/ISO_COBOL.md. 66 page breaks show the strict pattern (last line before the break indented >=3, first content line after it at column 0) — e.g. pages 78, 82, 178, 209, 214, 226, 274, 275, 276 — and 345 pages (27%) open with a bare list marker at column 0. The transcription OCRs each page independently and therefore carries no indentation context across a boundary. Ledgering page 961 individually would mean ledgering the same non-finding hundreds of times. (4) THE IMPLIED REMEDY WOULD MAKE THE FILE WORSE. The transcription inserts '', '## Page 961' and the running header between page 960's list and this continuation. An ATX heading terminates a list in CommonMark, so re-indenting '5.' by six spaces would not restore continuity — after a heading and a blank line, 4+ leading spaces open an indented code block, rendering two returned-value rules as monospaced code. Column 0 is the only form that renders as prose. The one genuine page-961 oddity I found is unrelated to this claim and equally cosmetic: line 38466 bolds the sentence-ending period, '(FUNCTION LENGTH (argument-1) + 1)**.**', where the PDF prints it plain. Recorded for completeness; it changes no meaning. This falls squarely under the rejection criteria 'the difference is only page-break furniture ... or formatting' and 'the difference does not change meaning'.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a discrepancy. All of page 961's text — items 5. and 6., 'c) Otherwise,', '(FUNCTION LENGTH (argument-1) + 1).', the NOTE and its three dashed bullets — is transcribed completely and verbatim, in the correct order, at specs/ISO_COBOL.md:38456-38472. The sole difference is leading indentation: the PDF prints 5./6. one level deeper than c) (verified in the 300-dpi render), while the markdown starts all three at column 0. That indent is dropped at page boundaries by the page-segmented transcription pipeline (66 of 1261 page breaks show the strict indent reset; 345 pages open with a bare list marker at column 0), the nesting stays unambiguous from the surviving '5.'/'6.'/'c)' ordinals against page 960's 1.-4. and a)/b), and re-adding a six-space indent after the intervening '## Page 961' heading would render the rules as an indented code block rather than restore the list. No meaning is affected; no ledger entry warranted.
